newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rwanda detains 5,460 over genocide, U.N. says.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda detains 5,460 over genocide, U.N. says.

text.p: Rwandan authorities detained 5,460 refugees returning to their homeland between November 15 and the end of last year in connection with the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, United Nations human rights observers reported on Tuesday.

The observers also gave details of seven deaths in five incidents between December 20 and 26 in southeasterly Kibungo prefecture, where tension is high between the local population and Hutu returnees.
They noted instances of ill-treatment in detention centres and illegal arrest procedures, according to a U.N. spokeswoman.

In a separate report, the U.N. Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda (HRFOR), while welcoming the start of genocide trials, expressed concern that the first two Hutu defendants sentenced to death last Friday had no defence lawyers.

Both men, who received a four-hour trial before a tribunal of three judges in Kibungo on December 27, were accused of organising massacres. They pleaded not guilty and have 15 days to appeal the death penalty.
U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut read excerpts from the two reports sent on Monday to U.N. High Commissioner Jose Ayala-Lasso, the world body's top human rights official.
"According to the U.N. Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda, 5,460 returnees from Zaire and Tanzania were detained as of December 31," she told a news briefing.
It was not clear whether formal charges had been laid against any of the returnees for involvement in the genocide.

Some 90,000 Rwandans are crammed into jails accused of having taken part in the massacre of 800,000 minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs. Over two million Hutus fled Rwanda in fear of reprisals for the killings.

More than 1.3 million Rwandans returned home in 1996, mainly from Zaire (719,307) and Tanzania (483,445), a spokeswoman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said on Tuesday. The rest came from Uganda and Burundi.
The majority those detained had come from Tanzania to the southeast prefectures of Kibungo (2,243) and Mutara (676), according to the spokeswoman.
Local authorities in some communes in Kibungo have responded to the large number of arrests by releasing people held for common law crimes, she added.

Tracing suspects on a government list of 1,900 persons accused of planning and instigating the genocide would be a priority for authorities in parts of Kibungo, according to the U.N. observers' report, which was not released in full.

"Primarily, it should be noted that the number of killings during the genocide was much higher in Kibungo than in Gisenyi and Ruhengeri Prefectures, where the majority of returnees from Zaire originated," it said.

"Unlike the camps in Zaire, where organisers of the genocide were reportedly able to take advantage of war conditions to escape, many organisers of the genocide (who took refuge) in Tanzania were unable to flee and were compelled to return to Rwanda," it added.
